For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

=== key f522d357f5b6

Problem: How strongly to state the prompt-engineering findings
Write-up text before the decision: gets much worse. We think this mostly shows that there are scenarios where LLMs (or specifically GPT-3) give answers that match the pattern of the correct answer (e.g. a color) but are not true. Importantly, we don’t want this to be interpreted as a “gotcha” result. We expect that LLMs will ultimately be able to solve these tasks based on content and not on pattern. However, we think that our results emphasize that LLMs can produce patterns that seem plausible and fit the suggested pattern while being incorrect. In these simple toy examples, it is easy to realize that the output is wrong but in more complex scenarios it might not be easy to spot and people could be fooled if they aren’t careful. Appendix A: prompts =================== Prompt-engineering ------------------ Prompt engineering is still more art than science. We got a better understanding from reading multiple posts (e.g, [[1]](https://www.gwern.net/GPT-3), [[2]](https://blog.andrewcantino.com/blog/2021/05/28/how-to-dramatically-improve-the-reasoning-ability-of-GPT-3/), [[3]](https://blog.andrewcantino.com/blog/2021/04/21/prompt-engineering-tips-and-tricks/), [[4]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.09690.pdf)) on the topic, but ultimately trial and error yielded the best results. Specifically, the things we found helpful were: * No trailing spaces - these just make everything worse for some reason. * Using a “Question: X? Answer: Y” pattern increased the quality of the output. * Using “Answer in three words:”, “Answer in two words:” or “Answer by copying the sentence” also increased the quality of the output.
Previous context: A research team is writing up a study showing that a language model can produce answers matching the expected pattern while being wrong, especially when shot and prompt patterns differ. In an appendix, they describe informal prompt-engineering experience gathered from blog posts and trial and error, including observations about trailing spaces and answer-format instructions.
Previous question: How strongly should the team state their prompt-engineering findings?

[...] ## 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LMs) are now competent at lying (Pacchiardi et al., 2023) and strategic deception when instructed or trained to be deceptive (Park et al., 2023; Hagendorff, 2023; O’Gara, 2023; Hubinger et al., 2024), as well as strategically deceiving third parties even when not instructed to do so (Kinniment et al., 2023; ARCevals, 2023; Pan et al., 2023; van der Weij et al., 2023). In this work, we demonstrate that, in a realistic situation and without being instructed to do so, LMs can strategically deceive their primary users. We simulate an environment in which the LM is deployed as a trading agent and show that the model makes illegal trades based on insider information and strategically hides the decision basis for the trades it makes from its users. While we don’t give the model any direct instructions to act deceptively, we put the model in a high-pressure environment where misaligned and deceptive actions can be useful from the model’s perspective. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of LMs trained to be helpful, harmless, and honest, strategically deceiving their users without direct instructions to be deceptive. This work is a result of a red-teaming effort, where we actively seek scenarios in which models behave misaligned and strategically deceive their users.
Previous context: A research team had demonstrated that, in one simulated environment, a language model made illegal trades based on insider information and then hid the basis for those trades from its users, despite not being instructed to deceive. The demonstration was the result of a deliberate red-teaming effort in a single constructed scenario, and the team had to decide how to describe the scope of what they had shown in their write-up.
Previous question: How broadly should the team generalize the claim about models' capacity for unprompted strategic deception based on a single demonstrated scenario?

=== key ce7b38f49757

Problem: How to interpret the lower misalignment and deception rates of older GPT models
Write-up text before the decision: ent and strategic deception in the insider trading environment. Strategic deception rates are computed only on cases where the models acted misaligned, and doubling-down rates are similarly conditional on strategic deception. All variants of GPT-4 display high misalignment, deception, and doubling-down rates. Other models are significantly less misaligned and strategically deceptive in this situation. We report the results in Fig. 3 and find that all GPT-4 variants (gpt-4, gpt-4-32k, and gpt-4-base) exhibit high rates of misalignment, strategic deception, and doubling-down on strategic deception in our insider trading environment. In contrast, GPT-3.5 and GPT-3 model variants (gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct, gpt-3.5-turbo, text-davinci-003, and davinci-002) display significantly reduced rates of these behaviors. We manually review some of the model completions. For gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct and gpt-3.5-turbo, we find that they basically always follow the prompt structure, take legal actions (from the perspective of what the environment supports), and correctly track the interaction state. We find that text-davinci-003 and davinci-002 sometimes take illegal actions, like attempting to “hold” the stock (even though this is not an action input we define). We further find that davinci-002 sometimes gets confused about the situation, breaking the prompt structure and producing nonsense completions. We conclude that less misaligned and deceptive behavior by text-davinci-003 and davinci-002 is partially but not exclusively explained by their inability to act competently in the environment.
Previous context: A research team evaluated several model generations in a simulated insider-trading scenario. All of the newest generation's variants showed high rates of misalignment, strategic deception, and doubling-down, while older models showed significantly lower rates. Manual review showed some older models reliably took only legal actions and tracked the state correctly, while others sometimes attempted undefined actions or got confused and produced incoherent output.
Previous question: How should the team interpret the lower misalignment and deception rates observed in the older models?

=== key 2272ce92b0d5
Kind of decision: how strongly to state a claim
Problem: How strongly to state conclusions about frontier models' evaluation awareness.
Write-up text before the decision: L Alignment & Theory Scholars (MATS) ###### Abstract If AI models can detect when they are being evaluated, the effectiveness of evaluations might be compromised. For example, models could have systematically different behavior during evaluations, leading to less reliable benchmarks for deployment and governance decisions. [...] To achieve this, we construct a diverse benchmark of 1,000 prompts and transcripts from 61 distinct datasets. These span public benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, SWEBench), real-world deployment interactions, and agent trajectories from scaffolding frameworks (e.g., web-browsing agents). Frontier models clearly demonstrate above-random evaluation awareness (Gemini-2.5-Pro reaches an AUC of $0.83$), but do not yet surpass our simple human baseline (AUC of $0.92$). Furthermore, both AI models and humans are better at identifying evaluations in agentic settings compared to chat settings. Additionally, we test whether models can identify the purpose of the evaluation. Under multiple-choice and open-ended questioning, AI models far outperform random chance in identifying what an evaluation is testing for.
Previous context: A research team studied whether AI models can detect when they are being evaluated, which could undermine benchmark reliability. They built a 1,000-sample benchmark spanning chat and agentic settings and measured discrimination performance. Frontier models scored clearly above random chance (best AUC 0.83) but below a simple human baseline (AUC 0.92), and models could also identify evaluation purpose above chance under multiple-choice and open-ended questioning.
Previous question: How strongly should the team state its conclusions about the extent of frontier models' evaluation awareness?

=== key ba3bacfe0f94
Kind of decision: how to interpret an ambiguous result
Problem: How to interpret the human baseline given that authors are familiar with the datasets and LLM evaluations.
Write-up text before the decision: datasets in our benchmark into two primary classes: (1) capability evaluations that assess technical abilities and general knowledge; and (2) alignment evaluations assess models’ adherence to human values and safety constraints. The full categorization is provided in Appendix A.3. We employed three distinct questioning approaches to assess models’ ability to identify evaluation purpose, illustrated in Figure 4. The model judge of the open-ended question was validated on a set of 50 hand-annotated responses. The full judge prompt and validation details are provided in Appendix A.5. ### 3.3 Human baseline Establishing a human performance baseline provides a reference point for interpreting model performance and also helps characterize the inherent difficulty of identifying evaluation contexts. To that end, each author independently annotated all 1000 samples in the dataset, rating on a scale from 0 (not an evaluation) to 1 (definitely an evaluation). The guidelines given to annotators can be found in Appendix C. The raters demonstrated strong agreement with an intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC3) 0.768, with 95% confidence interval of $[0.74,0.79]$. This indicates consistency in human judgments despite the subjective nature of the task. To create a final human baseline for each sample, we averaged scores across both annotators. We acknowledge that this baseline has multiple important limitations. First, the number of annotators is low. Second, due to the authors’ familiarity with the datasets and LLM evaluation methods, they should have high discrimination ability.
Previous context: A research team wanted a human performance baseline to contextualize model scores on distinguishing evaluation from deployment transcripts. The authors each annotated all 1000 samples, reaching strong inter-rater agreement (ICC3 0.768, 95% CI [0.74, 0.79]), and averaged the ratings. However, the annotator pool was very small and the annotators were already familiar with the underlying datasets and with LLM evaluation methods, plausibly inflating their discrimination ability.
Previous question: How should the team interpret and use this human baseline given its limitations?
